title: Dichroic longpass filter at 0 degrees
content:
Dichroic longpass filter at 0 degrees
This filter is the most important barrier to stop the laser light getting into the fluorescence detectors, while being as transparent as possible to the fluorescence emissions as close to the laser line as possible. There is a significant price difference between the best dichroic longpass filters and the mediocre ones. To resolve fluorophores such as GFP, BB515 and FITC whose emissions are close to the laser line, buy a filter that is substantially transparent at wavelengths > 500 nm. To avoid loss of sensitivity, optical density should be up to 6 at 488 nm.

title: Cytkit
content:
Cytkit is an open-source spectral cytometer. You can make your own, either from a kit or by sourcing all the parts yourself according to the configurations below. All mechanical parts are designed to be 3D-printed. You can also study and modify the design in free software (Freecad, with an ray-tracing optical model in the FreeCAD Optical Workbench).
The Cytkit instrument comprises: one laser, beam-shaping optics, a fluidic system with sheath flow and pumps for sample and sheath, optics for collecting and filtering emitted light, a dispersion element to split the emission into a spectrum, and flexural degrees of freedom to align the laser beam and align the emission to detectors. 
Cytkit configurations
You can configure your Cytkit with various detectors and acquisition electronics. These instructions cover two configurations as follows. There are many detectors and acquisition systems out there. We hope the community will try other products with Cytkit and share their builds!
Cytkit 1S-1F

This is the 1-scatter 1-fluorescence configuration, which uses electronics from test equipment vendors: 1 x amplified photodiode (Thorlabs PDA10), 1 x PMT (Hamamatsu H10732, 1 x USB oscilloscope (Picoscope 5000 Series), as well as separate boards for motor control, and power supplies. 

Note that 1 fluorescence detector is pretty minimal for a spectral system, to make an understatement! (At least you can mount it at a wavelength of your choice.) Moreover, the USB oscilloscope can only transfer a low rate of events. This configuration is intended as an demonstration for education and technology development, rather than as a workhorse cytometer.

Cytkit 2S-14F

This is the 2-scatter 14-fluorescence configuration, which uses the Astute Devices 16-Channel Cytometry Electronics Kit (2x photodiode board, 1x SiPM array board, 1x main board, 1x pump connector board, 2x interlock switches, 1x blower fan, 1x OLED display, 1x power supply, 1x set of cables). 
This configuration is intended as an easy way to build your own fully functional spectral cytometer. 

The Astute Devices 16-Channel Cytometry Electronics Kit is in development and anticipated to be released in Q4 2026.

Safety first

Cytkit uses a Class 3B laser (a 488 nm laser diode with output power of approximately 25 mW). This is hazardous to the eyes. We strenuously advise you to have laser safety training before building your own Cytkit. 

Suitable laser safety glasses that block 488 nm light are included in the bill of materials.
It is recommended that you do not switch on the laser unless it is contained within the main body of the Cytkit instrument with the beam blocked by the FSC detector.
The coarse alignment step in the build instructions requires working with an exposed beam (instrument cover off). You should take safety precautions for this step: 

check for stray reflections 
wear laser safety goggles that block 488 nm light 
ensure that no other people are likely to be exposed to the laser, for example by being in the same environment. 

The fine alignment and operational use of the instrument are with the beam enclosed (cover on). 
Two interlocks are provided in the Astute Devices 16-Channel Cytometry Electronics Kit to switch off the laser if the cover is removed.
Build Instructions
You will need the parts according to the bill of materials (, ) according to which configuration you are building. You will also need the following tools:

a set of Allen/hex keys
a set of precision screwdrivers

Unless you have purchased a kit, you will need the following in addition:

an FDM 3D printer (for almost all mechanical parts)
a resin 3D printer (for a few precision parts including fluidic sealing parts)

To align and test the instrument, you will need:

bright green fluorescent beads
rainbow calibration beads (e.g. Spherotech RCP-30-5A, Spherotech RCP-60-5, or Bangs Quantum 8-Peak)
fluorescein solution (optional)

title: Assemble the mechanics
content:
Assemble the mechanics
Step 1: Attach base to stand
Lay the base and stand on their side as shown. The stand is attached to the base with 4 x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 16 mm. 



Step 2: Attach main body to base, with springs under adjustment arms
First remove the printed brims on the ends of the adjustment arms of the main body as highlighted below.


Stand the base and stand upright. Then stand 4x Stainless steel compression springs, 0.5 mm wire, 20 mm length, 6 mm diameter into the circular recesses in the base as shown.
*** image of standing springs

Carefully lower the main body onto the base as shown so that the circular cavities under the adjustment arms capture the top of the springs without knocking them over. Then screw the main body to the base with 9 x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm. 


Screw in the 4 x M3 self-tapping hex socket cap screws 25 mm, first placing 1x M3 washers under each of the screw head. These are the lead screws of the adjustment arms, one on each adjustment arm. Do not fully tighten. Screw them in so that the adjustment arms are horizontal and the xy flexure stages are centred.

 
 
 
Step 3: Attach fluidics cart to stand
Working underneath the instrument, you may lay the instrument on its side again if you find it easier. The fluidics cart is attached to the stand with 4 x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm. 


Instrument mechanics assembled
Your instrument should now look like this. 2 flexure xy stages should be adjustable with 4 lead screws. 


Now move on to assemble the fluidics!

title: Assemble the fluidics
content:
Assemble the fluidics
Step 1: Assemble flow cell

Caution 
Take care not to damage sealing surfaces (barbs, o-ring grooves, o-rings, cuvette ends). Use plastic tweezers when holding o-rings (not fingers or metal tools).
Wear gloves to handle the cuvette: don't contaminate it with fingerprints.

First remove the printed supports from the flow cell. Take care not to damage the barb connectors.


Second, insert the o-rings at either end within the o-ring grooves. If handled gently, the o-rings should stay inside the grooves, due to a slight printed overhang. 
Thirdly flex the flow cell slightly as shown below to insert the cuvette between the o-rings. Tip: if using a square cuvette, you should be able to see through the cuvette side (with a magnifying glass) that the o-ring is sealing against the surface.

The flow cell accepts either a 4-mm round thick-walled capillary or a 4-mm square section cuvette. The round capillary has higher performance in fluorescence collection (less total internal reflection), but the cuvette has higher performance in FSC/SSC (lower scattering as the beam enters and exits the quartz).





Fourthly attach 120 mm of Silicone tubing 2 mm OD 1 mm ID to the waste barb on top of the flow cell, and thread this tube through the duct on the side of the flow cell so it sticks out of the bottom.

Note how the flow cell works and how it will interface with the optics. Inside the flow cell is a sheath flow chamber with concentric sheath and sample inputs. The laser beam enters and leaves through opposite faces of the cuvette, with fluorescence (and SSC) collected by a condensing lens at 90 degrees, and a camera viewport for alignment opposite the condensing lens.


Step 2: Prepare sheath and waste tank caps
The caps of the sheath and waste tanks must first be drilled with the right size holes to fit the required tubing connections. 
Note that the sheath flow is pulled by a vacuum on the wate bottle. Take care therefore to drill cleanly, especially the waste tank cap, as these holes must seal against a vacuum after fitting with connectors and tubing as follows.
Sheath tank cap:

5 mm hole (sheath tube), 
1.5 mm hole (vent)

Waste tank cap:

3.5 mm hole (vacuum pump) 
3.5 mm hole (pressure sensor or vent)
3 mm hole (waste tube)

Attach the following fitings and tubing to the caps, threading them from inside the cap as follows:
Sheath tank cap:

Bottom-of-bottle filter + 250 mm of Silicone tubing 6 mm OD 4 mm ID; pass through 5 mm cap hole from inside to outside, then add
Tube barb union 2.4x6.4.

Waste tank cap:

For waste stream: 50 mm of Silicone tubing 2 mm OD 1 mm ID + Tube barb union 1.6x2.4; pass through 3 mm cap hole from inside to outside, then add 480 mm of Silicone tubing 2 mm OD 1 mm ID.
For pressure sensor or vent: Tube barb union 1.6x3.2 + 400 mm of Silicone tubing 3.2 mm OD 1.6 mm ID; pass through 3.5 mm cap hole from inside to outside.
For vacuum pump: Tube barb union 1.6x3.2 + 400 mm of Silicone tubing 3.2 mm OD 1.6 mm ID; pass through 3.5 mm cap hold from inside to outside.

In the waste tank cap, push the tube barbs from the inside into the holes in the cap so that they seal. Screw the caps on both bottles. You can then put 2x cable ties on the bundle of tubing coming out of the waste bottle at 50 mm intervals to keep them tidy.







Step 3: Prepare and assemble sample loader
The sample loader is a linkage of several mechanical bodies that are printed in a single piece. Before using, it must be loosened and lubricated. 
To loosen the hinges, apply pressure to the two sets of adjacent hinges as shown. The outer hinges down and the middle hinge up. Alternate between the two sets. If printed well, very little pressure applied with the fingers should be required to loosen the hinges. Once the linkage is loose, add light lubricating oil to the hinges. Then work the linkage back and forth repeatedly until it can move with very little friction. 



<video width="640" height="360" controls>
  <source src="assets/20260814_113858 flex sample loader lubricate compressed.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Your browser does not support the video tag.
</video>

Attach the two sample loader range limiters to the holes as shown using 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm.
Attach the sample loader retaining spring (Stainless steel extension springs, 0.3 mm wire, 20 mm length, 6 mm diameter) with a 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm.



Finally, check that the SIP tube will fit in the sample loader: you may need to carefully ream the hole with a 1.6 mm drill bit. The SIP tube is a 78 mm length of Peek tubing 1.6mm OD 0.25mm ID. Cut the required length, straighten it if it was supplied curved, and gentle push it into the hole provided.


How the sample loader works 
The sample loader is based on a Kempe Kite Inversor 2 which is a parallel line linkage: it allows a single degree of freedom, while keeping the SIP and sample tube parallel to each other.


Step 4: Prepare sample (peristaltic) pump assembly
First fit the barb connectors to the peristaltic pump tubing.

Help Block 
if no barb connectors were supplied with your pump, these can be substituted with 10 mm sections of PEEK tubing 1.6mm OD 0.25mm ID.

If building the Cytkit 2S-14F, fit the stepper motor connector board to the pump, and ribbon cable to the stepper motor connector board.
Then fit the following tubing to the sample pump:

For flow cell sample inlet: 20 mm of Silicone tubing 2 mm OD 1 mm ID.
For SIP tube: 55 mm of Silicone tubing 2 mm OD 1 mm ID.
SIP tube itself (as described above).




Step 5: Prepare sheath (vacuum) pump assembly
If building the Cytkit 1S-1F configuration, first cut 2 x 200 mm wires for positive and neutral connections to the vacuum pump. Solder on end of each to the vacuum pump terminals. Leave the other ends as bare wire to connect to the screw terminals of the motor controller. 

If building the Cytkit 2S-14F configuration, the vacuum pump is already supplied with the correct length of wires and a connector to attach to the main board

Place the pump body in the sheath pump holder (flexible printed part). Then cut 90 mm of  Silicone tubing 6 mm OD 4 mm ID and put on the end a Tube barb union 2.4x6.4.


Step 6: Attach tubing to flow cell
Now attach the following:

The flow cell sample inlet barb to the open tubing on the sample pump.
A barb connector (or 10 mm length of PEEK tubing 1.6mm OD 0.25mm ID) on the end of the waste tube coming from the flow cell.
470 mm of Silicone tubing 2 mm OD 1 mm ID on the flow cell sheath inlet barb.




Step 7: Attach fluidics system to instrument
Insert the flow cell through the hole in the bottom of the base, and screw it tight with 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 16 mm.



Put the sample pump holder over the sample pump and fasten with 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm.

Thread the SIP tube into the sample loader and attach the sample loader to the base with 4x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 16 mm. Make sure the flexible tube from the SIP sits in the groove on top of the sample loader and is not pinched by fastening the sample loader.


Fasten the retaining spring with 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 10 mm.

If building the Cytkit 2S-14F configuration, screw on the sample pump connection board with 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm. 

Screw on the sheath pump holder to the inside of the stand (left hand side) with 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 10 mm.

Connect tubing:

Thread the sheath and waste tubing through the respective top holes in the left hand side of the stand. 
Connect the sheath tubing to the barb at the end of the sheath tank assembly. 
Connect the waste tubing to the barb hanging from the flow cell waste outlet.
Thread the pump tubing from the waste tank through the front hole of the second row of holes in the left hand side of the stand, and connect it to the barb coming out of the vacuum pump assembly.
If building the Cytkit 2S-14F configuration, thread the pressure sensor tubing from the waste tank through the remaining hole in the second row of holder in the left hand side of the stand.
If building the Cytkit 1S-1F configuration, insert a 30 mm section of PEEK tubing 1.6mm OD 0.25mm ID in the waste tank vent tubing.
Thread the dangling sheath and waste tubes through the serpentine retaining groove.




Step 8: Attach fan holder to stand
These instructions are for the Cytkit 2S-14F only:

Insert the blower fan in its printed holder.
Route the fan cable, the sheath pump cable and the pressure sensor tubing through the hole in the left rear of the stand to the electronics compartment behind it.
Screw on the fan holder
Check that the cables emerge at the rear of the stand (in the electronics compartment).





Test and check the fluidics
Make sure SIP tube reaches the bottom of a sample tube placed in the sample loader. 

Make sure the sample loader goes up and down smoothly, stays stably at both the top and bottom positions, and that a sample tube can be inserted and removed easily. You may need to straighten the PEEK SIP tube by bending it in the opposite direction from whichever way it naturally curled.

You have now build the fluidics system and are ready to build the optics!

title: Assemble the optics
content:
Assemble the optics

Caution 
Wear gloves to handle optics! The human hand is never clean enough to touch a lens or filter. Don't contaminate them with fingerprints.
You can use plastic tweezers to handle the glass optical elements. Don't use metal tweezers as they risk scratching or chipping the glass.

Step 1: Assemble laser holder and module
First cut of the brims and support tab of the printed Laser holder as shown. 
Second, attach the Laser heatsink to the laser holder with 4x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 10 mm
Third, screw the M9 mounted Laser collimating lens into the internal thread at the front of the 488 nm laser module . About 2 mm of the threaded mount should be poking out from the laser module.
Fourth, insert the Laser collimating lens adjustment tool (short) through the Laser collimating lens lock nut so that its two teeth stick out on the side facing the mounted laser collimating lens. 
Fifth, using the tool to stop the laser collimating lens from rotating, rotate the lock nut onto the mounted laser collimating lens until it gently locks against the body of the laser module, as shown.
Sixth, insert the laser module into the laser heatsink and tighten the two retaining screws gently.
Seventh, attach the laser module to the Main body with 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 16 mm at the front of the module, and 1x M3 self-tapping hex socket cap screws 25 mm with 1x Stainless steel compression springs, 0.5 mm wire, 20 mm length, 6 mm diameter at the adjustment arm at the back of the module.




Step 2: Assemble and mount beam shaping assembly
The beam shaping assembly comprises three optical components: Laser focus lens spherical,  Laser focus lens cylindrical and Band pass dichroic filter which are all mounted onto the single Focusing lens holder. The holder has a non zero angle of the bandpass dichroic filter to reduce reflections into the laser diode.
Firstly insert the components carefully into the focusing lens holder as shown. 
Secondly, attach the beam shaping assembly to the Main body with 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm. The screw attaches to the raised screw hole in the main body's laser alignment XY flexure stage through the slot on the focusing lens holder. Take care when tightening the screw: make it just tight enough to stop the holder moving, not so tight that it damages the 3D printed layers on the XY stage's screw hole.




Step 3: Insert condensing lens
First insert the Condensing lens into the Condensing lens holder.
Second screw this assembly only the main body's condensing lens XY flexure stage using 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm.



Step 4: Insert cylindrical correction lens (only if using cylindrical capillary)

Ignore this step if using a square-section cuvette.

First insert the Cylindrical correction lens into its Correction cylindrical lens holder.
Second screw onto the main body (fitting on the screwhole in the arm of the condensing lens XY flexure stage) with 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm.


Step 5: Insert neutral density filter
First insert the Neutral density filter into the ND filter holder for FSC.
Second screw the holder into the main body on the screw hole opposite the laser as shown, with  1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm.


Step 6: Insert dichroic and/or coloured glass filters

Here you have options depending on your budget. High performing spectral filters cost money. To achieve good sensitivity, one needs a high optical density removal of the laser light at 488 nm (ideally OD > 6) while letting through light in the band of sensitivity of the detectors, say 500 to 900 nm. 
The cheap option involves stacking a low-cost dichroic filter with a coloured glass filter. For less than USD 50 from Far-East suppliers (or about USD 200 from the major optics catalogue companies), you can have filters that achieve good sensitivity from about 520 nm upwards. However this loses the difference between the blue emitting fluorophores such as FITC, GFP and BB515.
For higher budgets, you can have a single dichroic filter here that achieves high blocking of the laser light while being substantially transparent at 500 nm and upwards. The well known quality suppliers are listed here. 

The Dichroic longpass filter at 0 degrees should have its coated surface facing the light source. Establish which surface this is by inspecting the edges of the filter with a loupe.
Insert the dichroic longpass filter and / or Coloured glass longpass filter into their respective holders. Depending on size, the following filter holders are available:

Circular filter holder (34mm diameter)
Circular filter holder (25mm diameter)
Circular filter holder (15mm diameter)
Rectangular filter holder (25.5x26mm)

Then attach each filter holder to the main body as shown using 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm.

If using a combination of a dichroic filter and a coloured glass filter, the dichroic should always be before the coloured glass in the optical train, to minimise the background fluorescence caused by the laser light in the coloured glass filter.



Step 7: Insert SSC focusing lens
First insert the SSC focusing lens into the SSC focusing lens holder.
Second attach the SSC lens holder to the main body as shown with 1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm. The space here is very limited for fingers, therefore it is recommended to use plastic tweezers for this step.


Step 8: Insert grating
First insert the Blazed reflection grating in the Grating holder. Make sure the arrow showing the blaze direction is pointing as shown.
Second attach the grating holder to the main body using 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm as shown.


Step 9: Insert spectrum focusing lens
First insert the Spectrum focusing lens in the Spectrum focusing lens holder.
Then attach the holder to the main body using 4x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm as shown.


Step 10: Insert dichroic beamsplitter

The dichroic beamsplitter (longpass filter at 45 degrees) goes straight into a holder which is part of the main body. Therefore be extremely careful not to break the holder, otherwise you will have to print the main body again!

First establish which surface of the Dichroic longpass filter at 45 degrees (beamsplitter) has the coating. You can do this by inspecting the corners of the glass with a loupe. 
With the coated surface facing the condensing lens, insert the beamsplitter into the slots in the main body. Tease it in very carefully! 

Step 11: Assemble and mount camera module
First insert the 5 mm laser blocking filter into the Camera lens tube then the F7D8 aspherical lens lens on top of the film. Make sure the flatter side of the aspherical lens faces outward.
Next screw the camera lens tube onto the camera module, leaving about 2 mm before it bottoms out.
Next screw the camera module onto the camera mount with 4x M2.6 self-tapping posi head screws 6 mm. 
Optionally add vertical adjustment to the camera mount as follows:

1xStainless steel compression springs, 0.5 mm wire, 20 mm length, 6 mm diameter in the camera mount between the overhanging tab and the base of the mount.
1x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm through the tab and spring.

The camera mount can now be adjusted slightly up and down by turning the screw.
Finally attach the camera mount to the main body with 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 8 mm as shown.






Check your assembly
Check that you have everything in the right place according to the images below. (Note detectors and the LED flash tool are described on the next page (electronics).)

title: Electronics: Cytkit configuration 1S-1F
content:
Electronics: Cytkit configuration 1S-1F
The Cytkit configuration 1S-1F uses entirely off-the shelf electronics to provide one channel of scatter and one channel of fluorescence. This configuration is primarily of use for education and technology development rather than as a useful spectral cytometer, of course. It may easily be adapted for alternative detectors and acquisition electronics. However, some skills in electronics are required to prepare cables and connectors, solder or crimp terminals, and choose power supplies.

Step 1: Mount FSC detector
Attach the Amplified photodiode (Thorlabs PDA10) to the PD module holder with an M4 hex socket bolt 10 mm. Attach the assembly to the main body with 2x M3 self-tapping posi head screws 12 mm.
The Thorlabs PDA10 comes with a BNC socket to connect to the oscilloscope, and a power supply socket for its own power supply. You require a BNC (Male) to BNC (Male) cable, 1 m.

Step 2: Mount PMT detector
Attach the Photomultiplier tube module (Hamamatsu H10732) to the PMT mount with 4x  M2 hex socket bolt 8 mm.
The PMT module requires a stable +5V, 0 and -5V power supply. It provides a stable 1V reference voltage for creating a variable bias voltage using a 10k potentiometer from the reference to the 0V pin. With some soldering skills and a Stripboard, one can make stable power supply with 8 x NiMH AA cells (approx 1.2 V x 4 for each of the +5 and -5 referenced to zero). One can also use a linear mode laboratory power supply with two floating adjustable voltage sources, where the positive of one voltage source is connected to the negative of the other. Use a SMA (Female) to BNC (Male) adapter to connect the module to the oscilloscope.
Separately, attach the PMT mount base to the main body with 2x  M3 countersunk posi-head 10 mm screws. The PMT module can be located according to a pin in the linear array as shown. Place the module at the 4th pin which corresponds to the emission peak of PE.




Step 3: LED flash calibration tool
This optional tool allows the calibration of fluorescence detector signals by an LED flash. Take one 3mm F3 round white LED and solder a 16k resistor to one leg. Solder a cable to connect it to a signal generator. When mounted, a 5 V pulse has approximately the same brightness in the PE peak emission channel as the brightest peak of the Spherotech 8-peak Rainbow Beads RCP-30-5A.


Step 4: Sample pump stepper motor controller
The Peristaltic pump for sample uses a 2-coil 4-pin stepper motor with a JST SH1.0 female 4-pin connector. The Astute Devices Cytometry Electronics Set includes a connector board for this pump, but it is quite difficult to find an off-the-shelf JST SH1.0 male with a cable. Therefore the most practical solution to control it is to cut off the connector, solder 4 wires onto it and attach a Dupont 4-pin female plug, which attaches to the Stepper motor controller board. 


Step 5: Sheath pump DC motor controller
Solder two wires onto the Vacuum pump for sheath as shown. These can be screwed into the Vacuum pump controller board as shown.


Step 6: Power supplies
The laser module, the sample pump and the sheath pump all require a 5 V power source. It is convenient to use a powered USB hub such as the one shown as a power supply, since each component can be individually switched. This requires 3 USB A power cables.

Step 7: Camera
The USB camera module comes with a JST SH1.0 5-pin to USB A connector. The camera mount and lens is described in the optics assembly instructions.

Connect detectors and controllers.
Mount the detectors as shown below. The mounting of the pumps and laser is described under fluidics and optics.
Connect the detectors to the oscilloscope. If you just want to see raw signals, you can use any oscilloscope. However, Honeychrome comes with a driver for a Picoscope 5000 series oscilloscope, which is convenient to record and analyse cytometry data. Attach the FSC detector to Channel A and the fluorescence detector to Channel B. Connect the Picoscope's USB cable to your host PC.




Now proceed with the software set-up.

title: Install and run the software
content:
Install and run the software
Step 1: Install Honeychrome
Honeychrome is an open-source cross-platform software package for flow cytometry data acquisition and analysis. It contains drivers for both Cytkit 1S-1F and Cytkit 2S-14F.
The Honeychrome package can be downloaded for Windows, MacOS or Linux, run from Python source or the Python package manager PyPI. See https://honeychrome.cytkit.com/ for full instructions.

Step 2: Install Picoscope software (Cytkit configuration 1S-1F only)
Honeychrome includes a driver to acquire data from a Cytkit 1S-1F using the Picoscope 5000 series oscilloscope. However this requires the separate download and installation of the PicoSDK from Pico Technology.
In addition, for the Cytkit configuration 1S-1F only, it is recommended to install the Picoscope software (Picoscope 7) for the Picoscope 5000 series oscilloscope can be downloaded from picotech.com. It is useful in the exploration and recording of data from the oscilloscope. It cannot be run simultaneously with the Honeychrome app.
Step 3: Connect to hardware and run Honeychrome
Connect your Cytkit via a USB cable to your host PC and power it on. Then run Honeychrome. Enable the Cytkit Hardware Tab by going to App Configuration > Bundled Plugin > checkbox "Cytkit Hardware".
If your hardware is functioning correctly, Honeychrome will report a successful connection.

title: Coarse alignment
content:
Coarse alignment
Diagram of adjustable elements
Note the following diagrams labelling adjustable elements (for both 1S1F and 2S14F configurations), which are referred to in the steps below.


Step 1: Safety check

It is your responsibility to work with the laser safely. Safety depends not only on the protocol that you are following, but also your experience, the environment that you are working in, the people around you who may be exposed to the laser, and your particular set-up and sources of materials.
A risk assessment should consider all of the above factors.

The coarse alignment requires working with an exposed beam. However, if you have followed the assembly instructions so far, the beam should be fully blocked within the instrument with no intense reflections escaping. The direct beam passes from the laser module to the forward scatter detector where it is blocked.
It is advisable to perform the coarse alignment wearing laser safety glasses that block 488 nm light, as direct visualisation of the beam is not required. 
Step 2: Focus camera on cuvette channel
Move the camera to focus on the inner channel within the cuvette. You can use your host PC's USB camera software, or the Cytkit Hardware > Alignment Camera tab within Honeychrome. You may need to adjust the exposure and brightness to see a clear image. Start with the camera tube lens screwed in fully, then turn the camera lens one revolution anticlockwise. Then move the camera in xy to an approximate focus and screw the camera down. Finally turn the camera focus slightly to improve the image. You should see an image like the one below. Depending on whether you are using a round capillary or a square-section cuvette, it will look either blurry (like this, due to astigmatism in the round capillary) or sharp. 

Step 3: Remove laser focus assembly
Carefully unscrew and remove the laser focus assembly as shown.

Step 4: Power on laser
For safety, ensure first that the laser is correctly seated within the instrument and the FSC detector mounted. 
Power on the laser by:

1S1F configuration: switch on the power directly
2S14F configuration: in Honeychrome, go to the Cytkit Hardware Tab, check that connection status says "Cytkit Connected". Then go to the "Light" tab. Check "Laser Enable", and uncheck "Interlock Enabled".



Step 5: Coarse laser collimation
Move the laser theta adjustment until you can see the blue laser light in the camera image. Insert the laser collimating lens adjustment tool (long) through the laser collimating lens lock nut and gently rotate until it finds its location locking against the collimating lens mount. 
Then loosen the lock nut by rotating slightly anticlockwise. Now holding the lock nut still, rotate the laser collimating lens adjustment tool until the laser reaches a focus as seen in the camera image.

Finally rotate the laser collimating lens adjustment tool half a turn clockwise to defocus the laser beyond the cuvette. Lock the lock nut. You should see that the laser spot occupies about half the height of the camera field of view.

Step 6: Replace and coarsely align laser focus assembly
Switch off the laser again. Carefully replace the laser focus assembly into its position. Screw in loosely but do not tighten yet. Now switch the laser on again. You should be able to move the laser focus assembly by hand to bring it approximately to focus in the camera image. Once that is done, gently tighten the screw to hold it in place.
Step 7: Laser focus / collimation coarse adjustment
Using a mobile phone camera, look at the diffuse laser spot image going through the laser focus assembly lenses. The elliptical spot's major axis should be vertical: loosen the screws holding the laser module within its heatsink and rotate the laser module within the heatsink until the elliptical spot is vertically aligned.


You should now be able to bring the laser to a focus within the camera image by turning the lead screws for x1, y1 and theta. The focused laser spot makes a narrow band of scattered light in the camera image as it enters and leaves the cuvette inner channel.

Step 8: Flow fluorescein solution (optional)
You can visualise the laser focus by flowing a dilute solution of fluorescein through the sample SIP. This allows direct visualisation of the spectrum on the array of detectors. Fill your sheath tank first with some suitable sheath fluid (e.g. deionised water or phosphate buffered saline). Dilute fluorescein in water (10 mg/mL) and put in a 5 mL flow cytometry test tube.
Switch on the sheath flow:

for 1S1F configuration, power the pump directly with the power supply and motor controller;
for 2S14F configuration, press the initialisation button in the acquisition widget.

Load a sample:

for 1S1F configuration, power the stepper motor directly, and with the stepper motor controller, determine which direction is positive flow into the cuvette;
for 2S14F configuration, press the start button in the acquisition widget.

Adjust laser focus theta so that the fluorescent light emission enters the detector. Adjust x2 condenser so that the fluorescent light is well focused at the detector.
To see the emission spectrum clearly, hold a white screen (e.g. paper) in front of the fluorescence detectors as shown.
<video src="assets/fluorescein spectrum.mp4" controls width="640"></video>

Wash out well with sheath fluid before moving on, as residual fluorescein creates a lot of background fluorescence. Load sheath fluid or water onto the SIP, then flush:

for 1S1F configuration, use the stepper motor controller to wash out the input line for 5 minutes;
for 2S14F configuration, press the flush button in the acquisition widget. Repeat several times.

Step 9: Mount fluorescence chamber lid
Place the fluorescence compartment cap in place.

Step 10: Mount instrument cover (Cytkit 2S14F only)
If you are building the Cytkit configuration 2S14F, you may now put on the instrument cover and enable the interlock again.
If you are building the Cytkit configuration 1S1F, do not place the instrument cover yet, as it must be off to access the FSC alignment in the next step.
You are now ready to move on to fine alignment.

title: Fine alignment
content:
Fine alignment
If you are building the Cytkit configuration 2S14F, fine alignment should be done with the instrument cover on (laser enclosed and interlock enabled). The cover is secured with 4x M4 Thumb Screws.

If you are building the Cytkit configuration 1S1F, do not place the instrument cover yet, as it must be off to access the FSC alignment.
Step 1: Flow alignment beads
To carry out fine alignment, you need bright green fluorescent alignment beads. Dilute them to a reasonable concentration (say, 1e5 to 1e6 per mL) in a 5 mL flow cytometry test tube.
Flow them on your Cytkit as follows.
Switch on the sheath flow:

for 1S1F configuration, power the pump directly with the power supply and motor controller;
for 2S14F configuration, press the initialisation button in the acquisition widget.

Load the sample:

for 1S1F configuration, control the stepper motor directly, flow at a low rate ~ 30 uL/min;
for 2S14F configuration, press the start button in the acquisition widget; flow at 30 uL/min.

Step 2: Signal check
When the beads pass through the laser focus, they will emit an intense flash of fluorescent light. Set Honeychrome to trigger on fluorescence: Edit > Instrument Configuration. Set peak detection channel to B1 for Cytkit 1S1F; B4 for Cytkit 2S14F. Set peak detection threshold to 200 mV.
If coarse alignment was successful. In Honeychrome (View > Oscilloscope Viewer) you should see something like the following: a rising edge refreshing several times per second. If you do not, gradually increase your fluorescence detector's bias voltage, making sure that the baseline stays below 100 mV.
<video src="assets/Screencast%20from%202026-11-19%2012-27-01%20alignment%20beads%20after%20coarse%20alignment%20in%20honeychrome.webm" controls width="640" type="video/webm"></video>

For Cytkit 1S1F you can also do the same in the Picoscope software. 
<video src="assets/Screencast from 2026-11-19 12-25-37 alignment beads after coarse alignment in picoscope.webm" controls width="640"></video>

If you don't see any signal like this, check the following:

Is the sheath flowing? (See if fluid is dripping into waste bottle.)
Is the sample flowing? (Can you hear the stepper motor / can you see its gears turning?)
Did you wait long enough for the sample to fill the input tube? (For Cytkit 1S1F, this is about 10 seconds of fast flow on the sample pump. For Cytkit 2S14F it is managed automatically by pressing start in the acquisition widget.)
Is the laser on, and are the detectors working? (You should see much higher background noise with the laser on than the laser off. In the oscilloscope, with subtract background unchecked, you should see a difference in the FSC level with laser on and off.)

If all the above are working but you still don't see signal, then coarse alignment was not close enough. Go back and check it.
Step 3: Align laser and fluorescence collection (fine)
While watching the oscilloscope, carefully adjust the following in order to make the flurorescence peak narrow in width (time), and bright in height (fluorescence amplitude). Ignore scatter for now. As the fluorescence peak height increases, lower your bias voltage to keep the peaks unsaturated.

x1 laser focus
theta laser focus
y1 laser focus
y2 condenser
x2 condenser

Your fluorescence peak should start to look like a clean Gaussian as shown below.
<video src="assets/Screencast from 2026-11-19 14-34-08 alignment beads after align fine fl.webm" controls width="640" type="video/mp4"></video>


Tip: Make your adjustments carefully: before turning each lead screw, make a mental note of its position, so that you can return to it if you go to far and the signal disappears. 
Don't continue adjusting blindly if the signal disappears! Searching for the laser focus after losing it is like trying to fine a needle in a 5-dimensional haystack!

Step 4: Align FSC collection
After aligning fluorescence collection, align scatter (FSC and SSC). Keep the trigger on fluorescence for now.
In the oscilloscope, uncheck "subtract background". Adjust y3 FSC until the FSC baseline is minimised. (Note the channel is inverted: minimising baseline here corresponds to putting the FSC detector in the brightest part of the beam.) You should now see peaks in FSC. If you reduce the flow rate to 10 uL/min they should become very regular in height.
If FSC is not regular in height, check the following:

Do you have bubbles / outgassing in your sheath fluid? (Are there bubbles in the sheath input line? If so, leave the sheath overnight for the gas to equilibrate, or pre-warm the sheath to ~ 40 C to drive out excess gas, and let it cool before using.)
Do you have a clog / debris in your flow cell? Try flowing cytometry cleaning agents before flowing the beads again.

<video src="assets/Screencast from 2026-11-19 14-41-05 alignment beads after align fine fsc trig fl.webm" controls width="640"></video>

You should now be able to trigger on FSC (Instrument Settings > Peak Detection Channel). Set threshold to 150 mV for Cytkit 1S1F or 50 mV for Cytkit 2S14F.
<video src="assets/Screencast from 2026-11-19 14-45-04 alignment beads after align fine fsc.webm" controls width="640"></video>

If you are building the Cytkit configuration 1S1F, you may now place the instrument cover. (You will have to disconnect the FSC leads and tuck away any other leads before placing the cover on. This is not necessary for the Cytkit configuration 2S14F where the leads are all enclosed.)
Step 5: Align SSC collection
To align SSC (Cytkit 2S14F), adjust z SSC until the SSC peak height is maximised in the oscilloscope. 
Your Cytkit is now set up! Move on to test it.

title: Test your Cytkit cytometer
content:
Test your Cytkit cytometer
Your Cytkit instrument should now be fully aligned and working with its case on.
Step 1: Flow alignment beads
You can flow alignment beads as in the previous step. In Honeychrome, you should see tight populations in FSC and fluorescence as shown below.


Step 2: Flow rainbow beads
Rainbow beads are commonly used as a check of an instrument's sensitivity, dynamic range and precision in a fluorescence channel. A commonly used rainbow bead source is Spherotech with 3 um 8-peak beads (RCP-30-5a), and 6 um 6-peak beads (RCP-60-5).

Sensitivity is tested by the number of populations that can be resolved separate from their neighbours, ideally all 8 in case of the Spherotech RCP-30-5a.
Dynamic range is tested by the number of populations that can be resolved simultaneously, ideally all 8 in case of the Spherotech RCP-30-5a.
Precision is tested by the robust coefficient of variation (rCV) of the brightest population.

Your Cytkit 2S14F should be able to resolve all 8 peaks of Spherotech RCP-30-5a in the PE peak channel. 


Step 3: Clean fluidics system
Congratulations! If you have got this far, your Cytkit cytometer is hopefully fully working.
To keep it working well, make sure the fluidics system is regularly cleaned to prevent build-up of a microbial biofilm in the sheath and sample lines and clogging of the cuvette.
The following generic cleaning agents are suitable. One should perform the detergent wash first to remove residues before the disinfection. Finally flush with water to prevent build-up of salt crystals or damage to the fluidics.

Detergent wash: e.g. Tween 20 (1%), Triton X-100 (0.1%), 7X detergent (1%), Contrad 70 (1%) or dish soap (1%) in DI water
Disinfection: 70% ethanol or isopropanol + 30% DI water, or 1% hydrogen peroxide in DI water
Flush: DI water

It is recommended to clean the entire fluidics once per month: load sheath bottle with each cleaning agent in order and flow each for 10 minutes with backflush of the sample line.
After flowing biological samples, it is recommended to flush each cleaning agent through the SIP for 2 minutes.
Step 4: Let us know your feedback
This step is very important! The Cytkit contributors have put a lot of hard work into this project, and we need feedback if it is to grow and continue. Please let us know how your build went, and any feedback or ideas.
